\section[maestus, maesta, maestum]{maestus, maesta, maestum — gloomy, mournful}

\label{lesson:LA-C269-maestus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for ready, then the Latin for facing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: maestus, maesta, maestum}
\textbf{maestus, maesta, maestum} — \textquotedblleft{}gloomy, mournful\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{maestus} belongs with \emph{maereō}, \textquotedblleft{}to grieve, to mourn\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), whose origin is uncertain.
\end{cousinweb}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for ready, then the Latin for facing, then say \emph{maestus, maesta, maestum} again
\end{itemize}

\section[ēbrius, ēbria, ēbrium]{ēbrius, ēbria, ēbrium — drunk}

\label{lesson:LA-C269-ebrius}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for facing, then the Latin for gloomy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ēbrius, ēbria, ēbrium}
\textbf{ēbrius, ēbria, ēbrium} — \textquotedblleft{}drunk\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ēbrius} may be inherited, from a Proto-Indo-European root \emph{*h1egwh-}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1); Lewis \& Short still called it doubtful. Its opposite is \emph{sōbrius}, \textquotedblleft{}sober\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ēbrius, ēbria, ēbrium}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ēbrius, ēbria, ēbrium}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{ēbrius, ēbria, ēbrium}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for facing, then the Latin for gloomy, then say \emph{ēbrius, ēbria, ēbrium} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does ēbrius, ēbria, ēbrium mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Drunk\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sōbrius, sōbria, sōbrium]{sōbrius, sōbria, sōbrium — sober}

\label{lesson:LA-C269-sobrius}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for gloomy, then the Latin for drunk.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sōbrius, sōbria, sōbrium}
\textbf{sōbrius, sōbria, sōbrium} — \textquotedblleft{}sober\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sōbrius} is usually explained as \emph{sē-}, \textquotedblleft{}without\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{ēbrius}, \textquotedblleft{}drunk\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1): not drunk. English \emph{sober} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sōbrius, sōbria, sōbrium}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sōbrius, sōbria, sōbrium}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{sōbrius, sōbria, sōbrium}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for gloomy, then the Latin for drunk, then say \emph{sōbrius, sōbria, sōbrium} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[avārus, avāra, avārum]{avārus, avāra, avārum — greedy}

\label{lesson:LA-C269-avarus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for drunk, then the Latin for sober.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: avārus, avāra, avārum}
\textbf{avārus, avāra, avārum} — \textquotedblleft{}greedy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{avārus} is built on \emph{aveō}, \textquotedblleft{}to long for, to crave\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): craving. English \emph{avarice} comes from its family.
\end{cousinweb}
